thread.title: Market 'Risk Off' Update Courtesy Of Bloomberg's Bond Page

author: DoctoRx
title: Market 'Risk Off' Update Courtesy Of Bloomberg's Bond Page
text:
Introduction - a surprise Thursday, the Bloomberg News bond page provided such a surprise that I wanted to share it with you, even though I just wrote a different macro article this week, The Good News In Tuesday's Selloff .
This is a sort of counterpoint to that article, beginning with credit issues, thus focusing on the potential bad news that could come as the Fed tightens credit and engages in the unprecedented action of drastically shrinking its balance sheet.
On the left hand side of the above-linked page (free registration may be required to view it), by the global bond tables are 5 headlines of related articles. Normally in a good global economy, most of these articles will range from very dry to neutral on the economy, even to positive (credit upgrades, falling default rates, etc.). This time, all 5 articles could have appeared on Zero Hedge , which is a haven for short sellers and predictors of gloom and doom.
When this sort of stuff has appeared in Bloomberg, it has paid to take it seriously, both on the upside and downside. I will discuss all 5
Two of the articles had the same theme:
Emerging markets could become submerging markets One was titled, Fitch Says EM Is Vulnerable as Debt Balloons to $19 Trillion . Fitch is a credit rating agency. The article begins with the main story:
Debt levels that quadrupled in a decade have made emerging markets vulnerable to tightening financial conditions in the era of rising U.S. interest rates, Fitch Ratings said.
Outstanding debt securities from developing nations have ballooned to $19 trillion from $5 trillion a decade earlier, the credit-rating company said in a report. Despite the development of local-currency bond markets, borrowers will be hobbled by higher external borrowing costs, a stronger dollar and slowdown of capital inflows, it said.
Where might the dollars have been made available to take EM debt from $5 T to $19 T during a generally weak period for the global economy? One guess.
That's right, it's quantitative easing, which bailed out the banks by "printing" (electronically) trillions of dollars of new money. Now, the Federal Reserve is in reverse, and these sorts of observations by Fitch are precisely what I have been expecting. So long as the Fed continues to shrink its asset base, the ratcheting effect will tend to produce stronger headwinds against foreign countries that borrowed in US dollars.
Bloomberg went on to add another article that made the above one look tame:
Worse Than 2008? Here's What the Emerging Market Numbers Show Harvard economist Carmen Reinhart turned heads this week with her comments on emerging markets, saying they’re in worse shape now than during the global financial crisis in 2008.
Her assessment comes at a time when investors are turning more cautious on the asset class -- and downright bearish on markets like Argentina, Indonesia and Turkey.
Well, we'll see on that one. I'm not that bearish.
My takeaway, though, is that the message is accurate: when the Fed is shrinking the base money supply and raising short term interest rates in an open-ended fashion, "safety first" is a source of alpha . Meaning, investments that are centered in the US and other safe haven territories with strong economies and reasonably prudent central banks is preferred.
So that's one type of 'risk off' strategy.
But...
It's not just emerging markets Italy is worrying markets, too:
Italian Markets Rocked by Reality of Populist Coalition Proposal -Strategists turn bearish with spread over bunds seen widening.
Apparently the incoming coalition government is talking about running huge deficits and possibly doing some sort of debt write-off. I don't have a full feel of whether this matters much to a US-based investor, but it certainly sounds like a USD-friendly, risk-off situation.
Next, much closer to home:
Forget FAANG-BAT stuff, it's company-specific now The idea that the 'B' (Baidu ( BIDU ))and 'A' (Alibaba ( BABA ))in "BAT" have anything in common with the 'T' (Tesla ( TSLA )) reveals just how much we are marketed every day in almost every way. Yes, all three BAT stocks move around a lot and have high valuations. But only TSLA has one operational and financial issue after another, leading to this Bloomberg headline:
Tesla May Need $10 Billion in Funding by 2020, Goldman Says Elon Musk may need to tap capital markets for more than $10 billion by 2020 to fund Tesla Inc. ’s auto-making operations, new products and expected expansion into China, according to Goldman Sachs Group Inc.
While Tesla has options to issue new bonds, convertible notes or equity, each choice would have downsides for investors, Goldman ( GS ) analyst David Tamberrino said in a research note Thursday.
With TSLA stock fading along with the lead that a normal industry ramp of its mid-level car, the Model 3, would have given before expected strong competition from the major companies arrives, TSLA's $48 B valuation now looks highly aggressive.
TSLA stock could go anywhere on the downside. Once the Street smells lots of dilution, that concept plus Fed tightening can change the mindset of investors quickly.
Then the caution may well be applied to other stocks, either stocks of well-functioning companies whose valuation is based largely on hope that its business plan will work out, or other companies that, as is the case with TSLA, have plenty of debt and also have significant ongoing business issues.
In the early stages of an economic upswing, when the Fed is making new money widely available, and again in 2013-4 following a sharp slowdown (QE 1 and QE 3 periods), these sorts of headlines usually are not too important. Now, 9 years after the Great Recession ended and with the Fed perhaps trending more hawkish than since 1981-2, all of a sudden, Goldman's $10 B can loom very large.
So that's another sort of 'risk off' consideration.
Finally, a reminder of the strange risks that exist:
Lots of marginal activities and marginal companies out there This is an oddball story:
Goldman Slashes Its Position in a Controversial CDS Trade A key player has had enough in one of the biggest credit-market tussles this year.
Goldman Sachs Group Inc. has dumped a big chunk of credit-default swaps linked to Hovnanian Enterprises Inc. ( HOV )...
That GE has now incurred "the wrath of regulators" is also mentioned in the article.
HOV is a troubled home builder.
This report raises more than one 'risk off' issue. One is a reminder that giant as GS is, it's involved in all sorts of smallish situations in its endless search for alpha and profit.Yet a small story such as HOV has angered a regulator. Hmmm...
Another risk-off set of points involves the specifics. First, why is a major banking company betting big-time on whether little, troubled HOV defaults? Second, while home building is in a bit of a boom period, it remains a tough business. Really, all businesses are tough. Many if not most public companies have numerous challenges. Many if not most stocks under-perform the averages not just by a little but by a lot. It's the big long term winners that really drive the averages to the numbers we see.
It appears to me that mid-to-late-cycle periods such as the US is in, where the Fed is aggressively trying to undo part of the inflation it so eagerly created in its ongoing QE's, is when the negative alpha from marginal companies begins to be created in large amounts. As per a Hemingway quote, the negative alpha starts slowly, then seems to happen all at once, such as during and shortly after a recession, or during a major sector slowdown as happened with the oils two years ago.
That's the final set of risk-off points.
How Bloomberg may be helping to point the way to alpha Combining all the above points, the very fact that Bloomberg's credit reporters focused on widely divergent bearish matters may be a sort of 'canary in the coal mine.' It fits well with the conclusions I came to a year ago, when the Fed began broadly hinting that it would perform reverse QE while also raising short term rates, namely to get ready for a period where caution rather than boldness would make the most sense. With a strong global economy and a business-friendly administration, the Fed's reverse QE has not harmed the S&P 500 ( SPY ) stocks at this point . But some of their business comes from marginal customers. Thus:
Weaker financial assets may have, in general, seen their peaks. If a storm, or storms, of unknown severity, are indeed brewing out at sea but headed to land, then where is the high ground? Where is the optimal mix of safety and prospective alpha from a longer term, total return standpoint?
I propose thinking of a geopolitical and economic matrix. Geopolitically, the US is the safest and has the greatest number of world-class companies. Next would be the strongest parts of the EU as well as Canada and Japan. Economically, the term structure of interest rates on the short end is still not very attractive, but it is getting more so in the US. On the long end, one can lend to, say, Microsoft ( MSFT ) for decades at a fixed rate of about 4% or less. Meanwhile, MSFT shareholders have a forward earnings yield (reciprocal of the P/E) around 4%; this is widely expected to rise at a good clip, thus soon enough it should be a 5%, then 6% earnings yield; and so on. If one has the constructive view of MSFT and the global economy that I do, then in due time, MSFT's earnings yield may get to 10%. Then wait for some more growth, and owners of the business can get 15%. Of that, perhaps a dividend yield on today's price would be 5% and share reduction would provide future leverage. All the while, MSFT bonds will be paying out at the same 4% rate. (I like the same types of numbers even better for Apple ( AAPL ), but picked MSFT because it's a triple-A credit.) My assertion is that big strong names such as these are the place to be for years to come, along with less-well-known strong names, especially if the focus is domestic or in the other safe/strong global economies.
The Tech Wreck, circa 2000-2, and the Great Recession were relative anomalies for markets and Fed action: each mess was made in the US. However, in the Reagan and Clinton presidencies - beginning with the Fed's dramatic easing in August 1982 that kicked off the secular bull market in stocks - over and over the Fed eased due to strains in emerging markets or other parts of the world. Fast forwarding from 1982, the 1998 easing was largely due to the financial strains in Asia and the collapsing economy in Russia. And post-Great Recession, part of what made the Fed perform QE 2 and possibly QE 3 were financial crises in the EU.
This is what I suspect the Bloomberg bond page articles are implying. In normal times, risk-off investing basically implies to sell stocks of all types and go to cash and/or bonds, maybe also to gold ( GLD ). However, bonds got caught up in risk-on trading due to QE as well as to low inflationary pressures. So while high quality bonds are safe enough, only a gloomy view of the future suggests there is any alpha from them any longer. The final 'but:'
Not thinking of bonds as a source of alpha is just one side of the equation. If Bloomberg's focus is correct - and it usually is when it's this one-sided - then emerging markets may have to accept a down-cycle for commodities they sell.
So they may not be a place to park money, either, and they are riskier than bonds.
Summary - 'Risk off' does not mean hiding Bloomberg's reporting is consistent with my view that the Fed is not behind the curve in its tightening program. I see the Fed's 6 interest rate increases, with a 7th nearly certain to come next month, and its accelerating shrinkage of its balance sheet, as beginning to bite. I would not be surprised to see some combination of strains in emerging markets and over-leveraged domestic borrowers stay the Fed's hand sooner than the market thinks.
Thus I propose that on the one hand, cash to be deployed when matters are more clarified makes a lot of sense, a "don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes" strategy. On the other hand, the outlines of the next up-cycle are already, I think, being foreshadowed. Increasingly, it makes sense to me to think of the 1982-98 period in which the Fed would have tightened further, but most of the time, something extraneous to the US stopped it (the major exception being the S&L crisis). This was the 'Goldilocks' period, aka the Great Moderation. In that period, the "right" stocks ran up, then ran up some more. Today, with competition from bonds so weak, we may be entering into that sort of period once again, though on a timing basis, we may still be a few months from the absolute best entry period. That sort of fine-tuning aside, a set of Reagan-type policies - toleration of deficits in favor of growth, military spending and maintenance of the social safety net - should allow secular growth stocks to provide alpha over the long term. Note, after the 1982 recession, long term interest rates rose the next 8 years, only dropping in the 1990 recession. There was no alpha from bonds, just the coupons, which were OK; but they are not so OK at today's rates.
Avoidance of the risky investments that Bloomberg's credit reporters have highlighted may, by subtraction from a portfolio or avoidance of inclusion, help lead investors to find their optimal mix of safety and alpha .
Thanks for reading and sharing any thoughts you wish to contribute.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL,MSFT.
